# Addressing the risk of monkeypox exposure during gastrointestinal endoscopy

Andrew Canakisa, Raymond E. Kima, Pranay Sinhab, Jean-Pierre Raufmana

University of Maryland School of Medicine, Baltimore, MD; Boston University Chobanian and Avedisian School of Medicine, Boston, MA, USA

Abstract The current monkeypox virus (MPV) outbreak is now a global health concern. MPV, a zoonotic double-stranded DNA virus, may be transmitted from human to human or by contaminated surfaces. Understanding the clinical characteristics and risks of MPV transmission are important, especially for health care workers, who may unknowingly encounter the virus while fulfilling their clinical responsibilities. The World Health Organization has recognized this orthopoxvirus outbreak as a public health emergency and the knowledge gaps regarding MPV’s transmission are likely to have contributed to its spread. Instituting proper infection controls in all settings, including the endoscopy suite, is critical to stemming this developing epidemic. Direct contact with skin lesions is the primary mode of transmission, and anorectal lesions are the most common skin manifestation. Hence, gastroenterologists and endoscopists are very likely to see patients with MPV infection. In this context, patients may present with symptoms of proctitis, or lesions may be encountered unexpectedly during anoscopy, sigmoidoscopy, or colonoscopy. In consequence, preprocedural exams and endoscopic procedures may increase exposure risk, especially if characteristic lesions go unrecognized. In this review, we provide background epidemiological and virological information, but focus on the potential risk of MPV exposure during gastrointestinal endoscopy and evaluate current practices regarding personal protective equipment and post-procedure instrument and endoscopy suite decontamination.

## Introduction

The current outbreak of monkeypox virus  (MPV; mpox) infection has raised substantial concerns at the World Health

Organization (WHO) and the United States (US) Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC); as of October 13, 2022, 72,874 cases across 109 countries have been reported [1]. As this outbreak progresses, it is important to understand the risks posed to both healthcare workers (HCWs) and the persons they treat. Here, we focus specifically on the potential risks of MPV transmission associated with gastrointestinal endoscopic procedures.

The prolonged incubation period, lack of adequate stores of vaccine, and knowledge gaps regarding MPV infection have all contributed to its spread. Instituting proper infection controls in all settings is key to stemming this developing epidemic. Endoscopy suites are no exception, especially as the close contact with patients during endoscopy may pose particular exposure risks. Although, to date, no cases of endoscopic transmission of MPV have been reported, our concerns in this regard were heightened when a member of our endoscopy staff was recently quarantined because of acute MPV infection; persons who underwent endoscopy in that suite within 10 days of this diagnosis were notified of potential exposure, although no specific recommendations were made.

Nonetheless, we must address the observation that MPV infection poses unique challenges that may require more specific measures. Virological and epidemiological characteristics of MPV

Whereas HIV lentivirus and SARS-CoV-2 comprise single-stranded RNA virions, MPV, first identified in 1970 in people residing in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, is a zoonotic double-stranded DNA virus belonging to the Orthopoxvirus genus in the Poxviridae family (Fig.  1, Table 1) [2]. MPV is endemic in western and central Africa and, following the eradication of smallpox, emerged as the foremost orthopoxvirus infecting humans [3]. MPV is highly pathogenic,

with similar manifestations to smallpox; yet, degrees of disease severity are often influenced by the route of transmission, host susceptibility, and quantity of viral inoculum (Table  1) [4]. MPV isolates are categorized into distinct genetic Congo Basin and West African clades. The current MPV outbreak is due to the West African clade, associated with a lower virulence and a case fatality rate of ~1% [5]. From 1970-1999, MPV outbreaks were reported in numerous African countries, with 404 confirmed and 500 suspected cases, but accurate reports are hindered in those nations by limited surveillance programs [6].

Prior smallpox vaccination appears protective against MPV; increased susceptibility to MPV in individuals born after 1970, following the cessation of the successful smallpox eradication campaign, may have contributed to the current rise in cases globally. The first MPV cases outside Africa occurred in the US in 2003, with over 70 reported cases linked to animal contact with an infected pet prairie dog. Despite small outbreaks in other European and Asian countries, research and funding have been limited [7]. As of late July 2022, over 25,000 cases had been reported worldwide, with 10 deaths (case fatality rate: 0.04%); as of September 30, 2022, the CDC reports that 26,049 cases of MPV have been diagnosed in the US alone [1].

The natural course of untreated patients is typically mild and self-limited to prodromal symptoms followed by a rash; yet a third of patients may develop complications such as proctitis, tonsillitis, paraphimosis, or abscess [8]. Immunocompromised hosts and delays in treatment probably contribute to the risk of MPV infection and mortality [9]. Patients can be treated with antivirals or vaccinia immune globulins [10]. However, our knowledge of the outcomes of those treated with antiviral therapy is limited to a small subset of patients in current studies, with no defined change in the natural disease course [7].

Clinical characteristics of MPV infection

The classical presentation of MPV mirrors that of smallpox, characterized by a febrile prodrome associated with mucocutaneous and systematic features (i.e., fever, lethargy, lymphadenopathy, myalgia, and headache). After the prodrome, skin lesions begin in the mouth, and spread to the face, trunk, and extremities. In the current outbreak, the clinical presentation has distinctive features: in 528 MPV infections from 16 countries, the initial lesions were limited primarily to the anogenital region, with later spread to the body, limbs and face (Fig.  1). Interestingly, most persons infected with MPV had fewer than 10 skin lesions, which can delay diagnosis [7]. Anorectal lesions can be associated with rectal pain, proctitis, tenesmus, and diarrhea [7,11]. Notably, in the current outbreak, systemic prodromal symptoms may occur only after anogenital or mucosal lesions develop. Thus, gastroenterology consultation may be sought before MPV is diagnosed, an important consideration for those referred for upper or lower endoscopy.

The median duration from exposure to symptoms is 7  days, and PCR data suggest mucocutaneous lesions may contain viable MPV particles for up to 21 days after symptom

onset [7,12]. Over 14-21 days after their initial appearance, skin lesions that began as macules progress to papular, vesicular, and pustular lesions before crusting scabs are shed (Fig. 1) [13].

Route of MPV transmission

MPV, a durable DNA virus, can be transmitted via human-to-human or animal-to-human contact, contact with infected body fluids and skin lesions, as well as contact with virus-contaminated fomites [5]. While prior outbreaks were associated with travel to endemic areas in Africa or contact with imported animals, the current outbreak has been primarily driven by sexual transmission, largely among men who have sex with men (MSM) [7,14]. MPV has been detected in seminal fluid and prolonged shedding was demonstrated in an individual co-infected with HIV [15]. In the previously described cohort from 16 countries, 98% of persons with MPV infection were MSM, of whom 41% were coinfected with HIV [7]. Similar epidemiology was noted in a UK cohort [11]. Sexual transmission may explain why the clinical presentation and symptoms in the current outbreak are distinct from previous descriptions of MPV disease.

As with the HIV epidemic, it is likely that MPV infection will spread progressively beyond the MSM population to infect others who come in contact with lesions or contaminated surfaces. In this respect, reports of nosocomial and household contact-associated infections highlight the need for caution among HCWs [16-18]. A  German hospital study identified substantial contamination of surfaces and fabrics in 2 MPV patient rooms [19]. The virus’s ability to survive for prolonged periods on surfaces outside the body is concerning, as objects in the endoscopy unit, such as bed sheets, computers, endoscopes and accessories, can serve as potential modes of transmission. An exposed HCW not wearing PPE developed MPV symptoms 18  days after exposure [20]. Given the aerosolization of respiratory secretions during upper endoscopy, MPV transmission via respiratory droplets is an important concern for gastroenterology and anesthesiology teams. Endoscopy and anesthesia personnel may be infected through viral contact with their mucous membranes, or by touching or otherwise contacting MPV disseminated on surfaces within the endoscopy suite.

Prevention, procedural modifications, and postexposure mitigation of MPV infection

Understanding the clinical presentation and modes of transmission highlights the importance of implementing effective strategies to prevent MPV spread to HCWs and patients. While ongoing clinical trials investigate novel treatments and vaccines, it is critical to develop protective strategies for staff and patients in endoscopy settings. Rapid detection, isolation, contact tracing, and vaccination of close contacts, all decrease the risk of MPV transmission [21,22].

Since MPV lesions commonly manifest in the anorectal area prior to the onset of systemic symptoms, gastroenterologists may unknowingly come into direct contact with MPV during rectal exams and colonoscopy. The potential for contamination in the endoscopy room represents a considerable concern. As MPV can also be transmitted by contact with fomites or contaminated objects and poxviruses can remain viable and infectious in the environment for days to weeks, there are concerns regarding the cleaning and handling of linens, counter tops, computer keyboards and screens, endoscopes and accessories. Our experience with acute MPV infection in an HCW is a case in point. Despite the low-risk exposure, since the individual infected with MPV was wearing PPE, all patients and staff were informed of possible MPV exposure. Following active surveillance and contact tracing, to our knowledge, there was no secondary transmission of MPV.

Nosocomial infections of HCWs not wearing or despite wearing PPE can be reduced through postexposure vaccination and active surveillance [23]. To prevent disease, if available, the JYNNEOS vaccine should be administered within 4 days of exposure. If given after this period, vaccination may lessen disease severity, but not prevent disease. Tecovirimat, an inhibitor of the orthopoxvirus VP37 envelope wrapping protein, FDA-approved to treat smallpox, is anticipated to be effective against monkeypox and can be used under the expanded access investigational new drug protocol. However, access to antivirals and vaccines may be limited, so recognizing populations at risk is important to prevent or limit transmission.

The COVID pandemic resulted in universal use of PPE, including N95 respirators, by personnel in endoscopy suites, likely to reduce the risk of nosocomial MPV transmission, especially following unrecognized exposures. Unlike HIV and SARS-CoV-2, MPV can be transmitted efficiently via contact with contaminated surfaces. Consequently, to avoid MPV infection, it may be prudent to double-glove and employ extra care when doffing PPE after leaving the procedure room. Post-procedure, the CDC recommends wet cleaning methods and advises against sweeping, vacuuming or dry dusting rooms, which can resuspend and aerosolize dried crusts from MPV skin lesions [24]. Furthermore, esophageal intubation or other procedures that expose oral secretions should be conducted using airborne pathogen precautions [24]. For waste management, the CDC advises that potentially MPVcontaminated materials can be handled as regular medical waste, similarly to soiled dressings or sharps.

There appears to be a lack of standardized methods for handling procedure-related equipment in centers where many HCWs and patients interact daily in a close setting. Reprocessing endoscopes is inherently a highly aerosolizing process through the flushing and brushing of channels [25]. Steam sterilization is not used, since the endoscopes are heat sensitive; instead, guidelines recommend the use of high-level disinfectants via mechanical and detergent cleaning, followed by rinsing and drying [25,26]. While there is no direct evidence regarding the effectiveness of disinfectants against MPV, there are abundant data on the effectiveness of common disinfectants, e.g., ethanol, hydrogen peroxide, glutaraldehyde and acetic

acid, against the vaccinia virus which causes smallpox. Soaking for 10 min in 0.02% glutaraldehyde, a disinfectant commonly used to process endoscopes, successfully produced a 4-log reduction in viable vaccinia virus [27]. While these data are probably applicable to MPV, direct evidence is lacking. Experiences with SARS-CoV-2 suggest that immediate bedside preprocessing of endoscopes may reduce or prevent cross contamination. To prevent aerosolization of viral particles, laundry suspected of MPV contamination should be handled in separate laundry bags and not shaken before washing at high heat or discarding [24]. The CDC provides guidance for MPV in the healthcare setting, with recommendations including proper use of PPE (including wearing gowns, gloves, eye protection, and surgical masks or N95 respirators) and single room standard precautions [24].

Fortunately, implementation of the more stringent changes in PPE associated with COVID-19 should provide adequate protection for endoscopy staff and patients. To our knowledge, no regulatory bodies are recommending additional changes to PPE based on the monkeypox epidemic. Moreover, as with COVID-19 policies, we mandated isolation of the infected staff member with active surveillance of those in close contact. In addition, given the lack of new monkeypox-related guidelines, we have not changed our routine policies regarding postprocedural room or instrument decontamination. Hence, unless we perform a procedure on a known case of monkeypox, we have not altered postprocedural endoscope processing or room decontamination. Of course, these policies may change as new information becomes available.

Concluding remarks

Within the past 40 years, after the HIV and SARS-CoV-2 pandemics, MPV represents the third major viral outbreak that the gastroenterology community must address. In response to the first 2 pandemics, endoscopic practices were modified by enforcing progressively more stringent use of PPE to reduce exposure risk to both healthcare personnel and patients. The potential risk of MPV exposure during gastrointestinal endoscopy is likely to escalate as the numbers of cases increase. We learned that a rapid response to possible MPV exposure, open communication with staff and patients, and post-exposure surveillance are likely to alleviate anxiety and reduce the risk of viral transmission. It is also critical to avoid stigmatizing MSM as we design infection control protocols. We anticipate that formalized guidelines from relevant gastroenterology and endoscopy societies will be forthcoming as the MPV epidemic progresses.

One significant drawback of food baskets is the uncertainty about PWTB getting an adequate 130 caloric load. Parents may instead prioritize their children’s nutrition, for instance. Gender 131 dynamics may also come into play. Further, time-consuming preparation and fuel poverty may 132 also inhibit the utilization of food baskets. And while Indian PWTB receive cash transfers 133 through the Nikshay Poshan Yojana, the impact of cash transfers on tangible nutritional metrics 134 among PWTB remains uncertain. RUTFs such as EDNS have been vetted in numerous clinical 135 studies for use in contexts such as severe-acute malnutrition.7 Providing a dedicated nutritional 136 supplement to persons with TB may help them attain a suitable caloric load, improving drug 137 absorption, and potentially reducing drug toxicity, relapse, and mortality, particularly if provided 138 promptly at treatment initiation.8 Moreover, the EDNS can be modified to meet the needs of 139 special populations such as those with diabetes. 140 141 This study has several limitations. First, as an open-label trial, the lack of participant and 142 investigator blinding may have introduced biases. Second, the study was conducted in two TB 143 units in Faridabad which may limit generalizability to regions with different socio-economic or 144 cultural contexts. Third, unmeasured factors such as dietary variations outside the intervention 145 or social determinants of health could have influenced the outcomes. Finally, the exclusion of 146 certain high-risk populations, such as those with diabetes or HIV, limits the applicability of our 147 findings to these key and vulnerable subgroups. More research is needed to optimize the 148 composition of EDNS for these populations as well as for children and pregnant women. 149 150 Our study demonstrates that EDNS effectively enhances weight gain among undernourished 151 PWTB while being acceptable and with minimal adverse events, offering a practical and scalable 152 solution for targeted caloric and micronutrient delivery. An integrated approach, as proposed by 154 India’s National TB Elimination Program— combining cash transfers, food baskets, and EDNS-- 155 may provide a more comprehensive and sustainable strategy to improve nutritional outcomes 156 and treatment success than any of these strategies. 157

ABSTRACT 47

Background: Undernutrition is the leading cause of tuberculosis (TB) globally, but nutritional 48

interventions are often considered cost prohibitive. The RATIONS study demonstrated that nutritional 49

support provided to household contacts of persons with TB can reduce TB incidence. However, the long- 50

term cost-effectiveness of this intervention is unclear. 51

Methods: We assessed the cost-effectiveness of a RATIONS-style intervention (daily 750 kcal dietary 52

supplementation and multi-micronutrient tablet). Using a Markov state transition model we simulated 53

TB incidence, treatment, and TB-attributable mortality among household contacts receiving the 54

RATIONS intervention, as compared to no nutritional support. We calculated health outcomes (TB cases, 55

TB deaths, and disability-adjusted life years [DALYs]) over the lifetime of intervention recipients and 56

assessed costs from government and societal perspectives. We tested the robustness of results to 57

parameter changes via deterministic and probabilistic sensitivity analysis. 58

Findings: Over two years, household contacts receiving the RATIONS intervention would experience 39% 59

(95% uncertainty interval (UI): 23–52) fewer TB cases and 59% (95% UI: 44–69) fewer TB deaths. The 60

intervention was estimated to avert 13,775 (95% UI: 9036–20,199) TB DALYs over the lifetime of the 61

study cohort comprising 100,000 household contacts and was cost-effective from both government 62

(incremental cost-effectiveness ratio: $229 per DALY averted [95% UI: 133–387]) and societal 63

perspectives ($184 per DALY averted [95% UI: 83–344]). The results were most sensitive to the cost of 64

the nutritional supplement. 65

Interpretation 66

Prompt nutritional support for household contacts of persons with TB disease would be cost-effective in 67

reducing TB incidence and mortality in India. 68

INTRODUCTION 73

Tuberculosis (TB) has regained its position as the leading infectious cause of death worldwide, with 10.6 74

million cases and 1.3 million deaths in 2022.(1) Undernutrition blunts the innate and adaptive immune 75

response to Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the pathogen that causes TB.(2) At least 2.2 million of 10.6 76

million TB cases are attributable to undernutrition, making it the leading risk factor for TB.(1) There is 77

also evidence that, among individuals diagnosed with TB disease, undernourished individuals face higher 78

risks of death, treatment failure, and relapse despite undergoing antimycobacterial therapy.(2, 3) 79

Historical data suggest that nutritional supplementation could have a beneficial role by reducing the 80

incidence of TB disease and reducing case fatality among those with TB disease.(2) However, in the 81

absence of contemporary empirical data, nutritional supplementation for persons with TB (PWTB) and 82

their household contacts (HHCs) has not been widely adopted. 83

84

The recently published RATIONS study randomized more than 10,000 household contacts of persons 85

with TB in eastern India between a control arm that received routine TB care with no additional in-kind 86

nutritional supplementation and an intervention arm that received macronutrient and micronutrient 87

support with a food basket that cost $13 per month for 6 months.(4) Compared to the control group, 88

the intervention group experienced a 40% reduction in TB incidence over the following two years. PWTB 89

in the RATIONS study, who also received nutritional support regardless of whether their household 90

contacts were in the control or intervention groups, experienced an approximately 35% reduction in 91

mortality compared to a previous National TB Elimination Program cohort. The RATIONS study shows 92

the potential nutritional supplementation to prevent TB incidence and mortality among household 93

contacts of PWTB. 94

Study Design 100

We used a Markov cohort model to estimate the long-term costs and health outcomes of providing a 101

food basket to HIV-negative household contacts of PWTB in India. We parameterized intervention costs 102

and effect sizes from the results of the RATIONS study, which was conducted among household contacts 103

of PWTB in Jharkhand, India, in a largely rural population with a high degree of multidimensional 104

poverty.(4) We conducted the study from the perspective of India’s central government, which funds 105

the National TB Elimination Program (NTEP). Recognizing that patient costs can often be substantially 106

larger than provider costs, we also conducted a secondary analysis to estimate results from a societal 107

perspective, considering costs borne by both patients and the Indian government. We programmed the 108

model using TreeAge Pro v.22.2.0 (Tree Age, Williamstown, MA). 109

Intervention strategies 111

We modeled two strategies. The “usual intervention” strategy reflects the status quo wherein 112

household contacts and PWTB do not receive any in-kind nutritional support. In the RATIONS 113

intervention, HHCs of PWTB receive a food basket that contains a daily multi-micronutrient tablet, rice, 114

and lentils for 6 months.(4) The food basket provides 23g of protein and a total of 750 Kcal calories daily. 115

In addition, under the RATIONS intervention we assumed that individuals progressing to TB disease 116

would receive a nutritional supplement that provided 1200 Kcal with 52g of protein for all six months of 117

Study Model 120

The Markov model simulates the natural course of TB incidence, cure, and sequelae for a starting cohort 121

without TB disease. The model was constructed as a set of mutually exclusive health states, with natural 122

history transitions represented by movements between these health states: development of TB disease, 123

TB cure, death from TB, and death from other causes (Figure 1). Parameters defining TB incidence rates 124

were specified to represent differences in the rates of progression to TB disease based on individual 125

nutritional status. Individuals developing TB disease could die, self-cure, or be cured via treatment. 126

Individuals who survive TB transition to an early post-treatment state, where they have an elevated risk 127

of recurrent disease for 12 months as well as increased all-cause mortality. Following 12 months in the 128

early-post treatment phase, individuals transition to the late post-treatment phase, where they continue 129

to have increased all-cause mortality, but where their risk of TB disease falls to baseline. We assumed 130

that after surviving TB, individuals would have a lower average quality of life due to chronic post-TB lung 131

disease. We used the model to simulate progression of a cohort of 100,000 household contacts of PWTB 132

through these health states over their lifetime, with a 6-month time step. 133

We employed the model to compare the RATIONS nutritional supplementation intervention to the 178

To assess the robustness of our results, we conducted both deterministic and probabilistic sensitivity 192

analyses.(17) For the deterministic sensitivity analysis, we defined a priori feasible ranges around core 193

parameter values (Table 1) and then repeated the analysis multiple times, each time varying one 194

parameter between the maximum and minimum of the feasible range, with other parameters held at 195

their point estimate. Next, we conducted two-way sensitivity analyses, in which we simultaneously 196

varied the parameters that emerged as the most important from one-way sensitivity analyses. 197

198

Lastly, we performed probabilistic sensitivity analysis (PSA). We defined uncertainty in parameter values 199

as probability density functions (PDFs) for each model parameter. We then employed 2nd-order Monte 200

Carlo simulation to repeat the analysis 10,000 times, each time drawing a random value for each model 201

parameter from its PDF. This produced 10,000 estimates for each model outcomes, with the distribution 202

of these estimates quantifying the uncertainty in model outcomes due to the combined uncertainty 203

from all model parameters. We report the PSA results using cost-effectiveness acceptability curves.(18) 204

In addition, we report uncertainty around main analysis results using 95% uncertainty intervals 205

calculated from the PSA results. 206

Sensitivity analysis 239

One-way sensitivity analyses for the general population showed that the two parameters with the 240

greatest impact on the ICER were the pre-recipient cost of the RATIONS supplementation (baseline 241

assumption: $28.5, range: $20-100) and the risk ratio of TB incidence for those receiving the nutritional 242

cost-effectiveness ratio for the RATIONS intervention was below to the WTP threshold ($550 per DALY 244

averted) when the cost of supplementation was less than $75, indicating that the intervention would be 245

cost-effective for any supplementation cost below this value. Even when we assumed the risk ratio for 246

TB incidence was 0.99, the WTP threshold was not exceeded. The model was less sensitive to the risk 247

reduction in TB mortality, the cost of TB treatment, and the disability weight for post-TB lung disease 248

(Table 4). 249

DISCUSSION 265

Nutritional interventions to mitigate risks of TB incidence and mortality are often perceived to be cost 266

prohibitive. However, the RATIONS study has provided empirical evidence that low-cost nutritional 267

support could have a substantial impact on lowering the risk of incident TB in settings with high rates of 268

multidimensional poverty and undernutrition. Our analysis suggests that an in-kind nutritional 269

intervention modelled on the food basket used in the RATIONS study could be cost-effective for 270

reducing TB incidence and mortality in India. We estimated that RATIONS-style nutritional support 271

would have a cost-effectiveness of $229 per DALY averted from a healthcare perspective and $184 per 272

DALY averted from a societal perspective. Our findings can help national TB programs as they consider 273

the economics of implementing nutritional support to reduce the incidence of TB among household 274

contacts. 275

276

Balanced nutritional interventions likely reduce incident TB disease by enhancing the humoral and 277

innate responses to Mycobacterium tuberculosis; these responses can help infected individuals 278

eliminate or contain the bacilli.(2) Nutritional support to malnourished individuals may acutely restore 279

their immune response. Indeed, mouse models suggest that providing a protein-rich diet to protein- 280

deficient mice can restore their anti-tubercular immune response within two weeks.(19) Given that the 281

majority of TB disease in high burden settings arises from infection within the past two years, nutritional 282

support should be provided to HHCs promptly after the diagnosis of the index case to prevent incident 283

TB disease.(20) 284

In our model, we limited the reduction in TB incidence among HHCs to two years after exposure since 286

this was the duration of follow-up observed in the RATIONS study. For subsequent years, we assumed 287

that individuals receiving the RATIONS intervention would have the same incidence rate as the usual 288

care group, which remained elevated in years 3, 4, and 5 since exposure. Given the impact of nutritional 289

support on the immune response to TB, it is possible that individuals receiving improved nutrition are 290

more resistant to new TB infection. If so, the incidence reductions produced by the RATIONS 291

intervention could extend beyond the two years assumed in this analysis. As such, our health impact and 292

cost-effectiveness estimates may be conservative. 293

294

It is important to note that that the RATIONS study—on which this cost-effectiveness analysis was 295

based—was conducted in a population with high levels of material deprivation and undernutrition, and 296

TB incidence rates higher than those estimated for other parts of India. It is possible that the impact and 297

cost-effectiveness of nutritional support may be lower in settings with a lower prevalence and severity 298

of undernutrition, or lower TB incidence. Our two-way sensitivity analysis suggests that even at the 299

lowest estimates of risk reduction for TB incidence (15% reduction) and mortality (15% reduction), the 300

intervention would remain below the WTP threshold. These are credible effect sizes in less 301

impoverished populations. A systematic review, which largely drew on data from high income countries, 302

found a log-linear relationship between BMI and TB incidence wherein TB incidence decreases by 303

approximately 14% per 1kg/m2 increase in BMI which is entirely achievable in 6 months on the RATIONS 304

intervention. Further, a systematic review of randomized trials of macronutrient supplementation in 305

PWTB, despite being underpowered, estimated that macronutrient supplementation was associated 306

with a RR of 0.34 (95% CI: 0.10–1.20) for TB mortality.(21) 307

Public health investments to eliminate TB and undernutrition have historically provided some of the 309

greatest returns on investment.(22, 23) The ICER estimated for nutritional support in our study is 310

considerably below both the country-specific WTP threshold for India and the ICER for well-accepted TB 311

preventive interventions, such as test-driven isoniazid preventive therapy for persons with HIV/AIDS 312

($1154 per DALY averted).(24) In our model, the ICER was most sensitive to the cost of nutritional 313

supplementation for HHCs. Even when we assumed the lowest possible effect of nutritional 314

interventions on incident TB disease, nutritional support would be cost-effective at $56 per recipient 315

over 6 months, which was nearly twice the cost of the intervention. It is possible that state and national 316

governments would enjoy economies of scale, not possible in the context of a clinical trial, that 317

consequently could further lower the cost of the intervention. 318

319

Our analysis has several limitations. First, we did not model the impact of nutritional interventions on 320

reducing early relapses and disengagement from care, even though these are plausible effects.(2, 25) 321

Second, we did not account for reductions in TB transmission and secondary TB cases that might result 322

from lower TB incidence, and instead focused on the direct health benefits experienced by intervention 323

recipients. Third, our cost assumptions were limited to drug-susceptible TB, which is less costly to treat 324

than drug-resistant TB, (13) and we also did not model the medical and non-medical costs faced by 325

PWTB prior to their diagnosis. Approximately two-thirds of Indian PWTB treated in the public sector first 326

seek care in the private sector and accrue large costs before an accurate TB diagnosis is made.(13) Forth, 327

the model did not capture the positive externalities of nutritional support, including improvements in 328

nutritional status and functional recovery and improved economic productivity among TB survivors, 329

which have been explored in a previous analysis.(26) Taken together, these limitations suggest that our 330

ICER estimates will be conservative, and that nutritional support could be even more cost-effective than 331

we project. 332

Improvements in population-level nutrition and progress on social determinants of health likely 334

contributed to the massive decline in TB incidence and mortality in countries like the United States and 335

the United Kingdom that occurred even prior to the introduction of antimicrobials.(25) The striking 336

findings of the RATIONS study have demonstrated the role nutritional interventions can play in the 337

contemporary era to accelerate TB elimination. India is well positioned to institute a large-scale 338

nutritional support program as it already has well-established infrastructure for delivering in-kind 339

rations, mid-day meals, and nutritional counseling.(27-29) The TB Mitra Program, which crowdsources 340

nutritional support for persons with TB, could also be scaled up.(30) 341

342

Additional research is necessary to help us understand how to target nutritional interventions equitably 343

and efficiently. Operational studies are needed to design optimal delivery systems. Even as nutritional 344

interventions are operationalized in settings with lower prevalence of undernutrition in India, 345

epidemiological studies can help us understand the effect size of nutritional interventions in diverse 346

populations. We also need clinical and translational studies to better define the nutritional needs of 347

special populations, such as pregnant women and children, to develop the best possible nutritional 348

package. Economic evaluations should be conducted alongside nutritional intervention studies to inform 349

policy. 350

351

In conclusion, our analysis projected that a RATIONS-style intervention would be cost-effective for 352

populations with a high dual burden of TB and undernutrition in India and drive large reductions in TB 353

incidence and mortality among household contacts of persons with TB. 354

# In-kind nutritional supplementation for persons with drug-susceptible tuberculosis and their household contacts would be cost-effective for reducing tuberculosis incidence and mortality in Jharkhand, India: a modeling study

**Authors:** Pranay Sinha; Madhavi Bhargava; Madolyn Dauphinais; Madeline E. Carwile; C. Robert Horsburgh; Urvashi B. Singh; Sonali Sarkar; Anurag Bhargava; Nicolas A. Menzies

## Abstract

Undernutrition is the leading cause of tuberculosis (TB) globally, but nutritional interventions are often considered cost-prohibitive. The RATIONS study demonstrated that nutritional supplementation to household contacts of persons with TB can reduce TB incidence, yet economic evaluations of such strategies remain limited.

Using a Markov model, we assessed the cost-effectiveness of a RATIONS-style intervention (monthly food basket providing 750 kcal, 23g of protein, and a multi-micronutrient tablet daily) for household contacts of persons with TB, as compared to no nutritional support. We calculated health outcomes (TB episodes, TB deaths, and disability-adjusted life years [DALYs]) over the lifetime of intervention recipients and assessed costs from healthcare and societal perspectives. We tested the robustness of results to parameter changes via deterministic and probabilistic sensitivity analysis.

Over two years, household contacts receiving the RATIONS intervention experienced 38% (95% uncertainty interval [UI]: 23–52) fewer TB episodes and 58% (95% UI: 44–70) fewer TB deaths. Over the lifetime of a cohort of 100,000 household contacts, the intervention was projected to avert 11,524 DALYs (95% UI: 7,446–17,393) and was cost-effective from both the healthcare (incremental cost-effectiveness ratio [ICER]: $289 per DALY averted [95% UI: 156–537]) and societal perspectives ($229 per DALY averted [95% UI: 102–468]). Cost-effectiveness was most sensitive to the cost of the nutritional supplement.

Prompt nutritional support for household contacts of persons with TB disease would be cost-effective in reducing TB incidence and mortality in India.

## INTRODUCTION

Tuberculosis (TB) is the leading infectious cause of death worldwide, with 10.8 million persons experiencing TB disease and 1.25 million TB deaths in 2023.(1) Undernutrition weakens the immune response to Mycobacterium tuberculosis and is the leading risk factor for TB globally.(2) Undernourished PWTB face higher risks of death, treatment failure, and relapse despite undergoing antimycobacterial therapy.(2, 3)

The RATIONS (Reducing Activation of Tuberculosis by Improvement of Nutritional Status) study randomized more than 10,000 household contacts (HHCs) of persons with tuberculosis (PWTB) in the Indian state of Jharkhand between a control arm that received routine TB care with no additional in-kind nutritional supplementation and an intervention arm that received macronutrient and micronutrient support with an inexpensive food basket for six months.(4) PWTB in both arms received nutritional support. Compared to the control group, the intervention group experienced a nearly 40% reduction in TB incidence over the following two years. PWTB in the RATIONS study, who also received nutritional support regardless of whether their HHCs were in the control or intervention groups, experienced an approximately 35% reduction in mortality compared to a previous National TB Elimination Program (NTEP) cohort.(5)

We developed a Markov state transition model to explore if a RATIONS-style nutritional intervention would be cost-effective for reducing TB incidence and mortality in Jharkhand.

## METHODS

### Study Design

We developed a Markov cohort model to estimate the long-term costs and health outcomes of providing a food basket to HHCs of PWTB in India, following current best-practice guidelines for cost-effectiveness modelling.(6, 7) We parameterized intervention costs and effect sizes from the results of the RATIONS study, which was conducted among HHCs of PWTB in Jharkhand, India, in a largely rural population with a high degree of multidimensional poverty.(4) We conducted the study from the healthcare perspective. Recognizing that societal costs can often be substantially higher than provider costs, we also conducted a secondary analysis to estimate results from a societal perspective, considering costs borne by both PWTB and the Indian government which funds the NTEP. We programmed the model using TreeAge Pro v.22.2.0 (Tree Age, Williamstown, MA).

### Model Population

Our modeled population resembled the HHC cohort enrolled in the RATIONS study conducted in Jharkhand, India. Full details of this population have been described elsewhere, but briefly: the median age was 21.5 years (IQR: 11.0–36.8), and undernutrition was highly prevalent—38.3% of individuals receiving nutritional support met age-appropriate criteria for undernutrition.(4) Only 0.15% were living with HIV. These values informed our model assumptions regarding baseline nutritional status and age structure in the HHC population.

### Intervention strategies

We modeled two strategies. The “usual intervention” strategy reflects the status quo, wherein HHCs and PWTB do not receive any in-kind nutritional support. In the RATIONS intervention, PWTB received a nutritional supplement that provided 1200 Kcal with 52g of protein for all six months of TB treatment.(4) HHCs of PWTB receive a food basket containing a daily multi-micronutrient tablet, rice, and lentils that provide 23g of protein and a total of 750 Kcal daily.

### Study Model

The Markov model was designed to simulate the natural course of TB incidence, treatment, and long-term sequelae for a starting cohort without TB disease. It comprised a set of mutually exclusive health states in six-month time steps: development of TB disease, TB cure, death from TB, and death from other causes (Figure 1).

Importantly, TB disease was modeled as a transition event rather than a persistent health state. Individuals who developed TB disease either died within the same time step (based on fatality rate assumptions) or were assumed to be diagnosed and cured—either through treatment or spontaneous recovery—and then entered the early post-treatment state. This structure allowed the model to explicitly capture TB incidence, recurrence, and TB-related mortality, while maintaining parsimony.

Individuals who survived TB entered the early post-treatment state, where they experienced elevated risk of recurrent TB and increased all-cause mortality for 12 months. After this period, they transitioned to the late post-treatment state, where recurrence risk returned to baseline but excess mortality persisted. We assumed that all TB survivors had reduced quality of life due to chronic post-TB lung disease. The model simulated the lifetime trajectory of a cohort of 100,000 HHCs of persons with TB (PWTB) across these health states.

### Parameter Inputs

#### Health Outcomes

Outcomes of interest from the simulation included TB disease incidence, TB deaths, disability-adjusted life years (DALYs), and costs from the healthcare perspective. In a secondary analysis, we also considered costs from a societal perspective. All outcomes were assessed over the lifetime of the modeled cohort.

We sourced TB incidence rates for HHCs after exposure from a previous meta-analysis.(8) Table 1 presents incidence estimates adopted for the analysis for the first five years. After five years of elevated risk of TB disease, we assumed the incidence would drop to prevailing rates in Jharkhand: 130/100,000 as reported in the RATIONS study.(4) Given that substate variations are possible, we conducted sensitivity analysis with a lower incidence of 65/100,000 and a higher incidence of 390/100,000 as well. To account for the long-term secular declines in the incidence of TB in the population, we assumed a 3% annual decline based on incidence trends estimated for India over the past five years based on data from the WHO global TB report (1) (Supplementary table 1). In the early post-treatment phase, we assumed that TB survivors had an increased risk of recurrent TB based on observed data from India.(5) In the late post-treatment phase, the risk dropped to baseline.

We obtained TB fatality rates from the WHO Global TB Report 2022.(3) Using WHO life tables for background mortality rates, we constructed TB-deleted life tables.(9) For individuals surviving TB, we estimated a lifetime increase in TB-attributable mortality using previous conservative estimates.(10)

To calculate DALYs, we applied an annual disability weight of 0.333 (95% CI: 0.224–0.454), based on the Global Burden of Disease Study 2019, for 6 months to represent the symptomatic phase of TB disease, and a disability weight of 0.053 (95% CI: 0.026–0.079), from Quaife et al. (2020), for the remainder of life expectancy among those cured of TB.(11, 12)

#### Intervention impact

We assumed prompt nutritional supplementation would reduce the risk of incident TB disease among HHCs. Based on the results of the RATIONS study, we assumed an incidence rate ratio of 0·61 (95% CI 0·43, 0·85) for HHCs receiving supplementation compared to no supplementation for two years from the beginning of the intervention. After two years, we assumed that those receiving the intervention and those receiving usual care had a similar risk of incident TB disease. If HHCs developed TB disease during the model horizon, we assumed they would then receive nutritional support PWTB, which would reduce TB-related mortality. This mortality benefit was based on a comparison of outcomes of PWTB in the RATIONS study to an NTEP cohort, which yielded a risk ratio (RR) of 0·65 (95% CI: 0·49, 0·85).(5, 13) We did not model the mortality benefit for the index PWTB.

We used cost data from the RATIONS study, which reported supplementation costs of $14.7 per month, including delivery costs for PWTB and $4.75 per month for each HHC. In sensitivity analyses, we examined a wide range of values for the cost of nutritional supplementation to account for regional variation, diversion of food grains, and wastage. We obtained TB treatment costs from a microcosting study.(14) For costs borne by PWTB and affected households, we assumed that the direct medical costs, direct non-medical costs, and productivity losses borne by TB-affected households would be $700 (SD: 140) per TB episode.(15, 16) We rounded all costs to the nearest dollar. All costs are reported in 2024 US dollars.

### Cost-effectiveness analysis

We calculated incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs) as the ratio of mean incremental costs to mean incremental health benefits (DALYs averted) for the intervention compared to the usual care strategy. Costs and DALYs were discounted at 3% per annum.(17)

#### Willingness-to-pay

We derived our willingness-to-pay (WTP) threshold from Ochalek et al., who estimated country-specific willingness-to-pay thresholds based on the opportunity cost of healthcare spending.(18) For India, this study estimated a WTP threshold equivalent to 23% of per-capita GDP (US$570 in 2024). We considered ICERs below this threshold to be cost-effective.

### Sensitivity analysis

To assess the robustness of our results, we conducted both deterministic and probabilistic sensitivity analyses.(19) For the deterministic sensitivity analysis, we defined a priori feasible ranges around core parameter values (Table 1). Then, we repeated the analysis multiple times, each time varying one parameter between the maximum and minimum of the feasible range, with other parameters held at their point estimate. Next, we conducted two-way sensitivity analyses, in which we simultaneously varied the parameters that emerged as the most important from one-way sensitivity analyses.

Lastly, we performed probabilistic sensitivity analysis (PSA). We defined uncertainty in parameter values as probability density functions (PDFs) for each model parameter. We then employed 2nd-order Monte Carlo simulation to repeat the analysis 10,000 times, each time drawing a random value for each model parameter from its PDF. This produced 10,000 estimates for each model outcome, with the distribution of these estimates quantifying the uncertainty in model outcomes due to the combined uncertainty from all model parameters. We report the PSA results using cost-effectiveness acceptability curves.(20) In addition, we report uncertainty around the main analysis results using equal-tailed 95% uncertainty intervals (UI) calculated from the PSA results.

## RESULTS

### Primary model results

Primary model results are presented in Table 2. Per 100,000 HHCs, those receiving the RATIONS intervention experienced fewer cumulative TB episodes (6958 vs. 7882) and TB-related deaths (651 vs. 1097) over their lifetime, corresponding to 924 TB episodes and 446 TB deaths averted. These differences reflect a risk ratio (RR) of 0.88 (95% UI: 0.83–0.93) for TB incidence and 0.59 (95% UI: 0.49–0.71) for TB mortality. In the first two years of this model, there were 1634 TB episodes (95% UI: 1069–2450) in the RATIONS intervention as opposed to 2594 TB episodes (95% UI: 1913–3651) with usual care, RR 0.62 (0.48–0.77). These results are consistent with the empirical findings of the RATIONS trial. The RATIONS intervention averted 11,524 DALYs per 100,000 individuals compared to usual care, with most of the health gains attributable to reductions in TB mortality (Table 3).

From the healthcare perspective, total discounted costs per 100,000 individuals were $0.84 million (95% UI: 0.52–1.41) under usual care—reflecting TB treatment costs—and $4.24 million (95% UI: 3.07–5.64) under the RATIONS intervention, of which $0.72 million (95% UI: 0.44–1.23) was for TB care and the remainder for nutritional support. From the societal perspective, total costs were $5.72 million (95% UI: 3.86–9.23) for the usual care strategy. Total societal costs under the RATIONS intervention were $8.45 million (95% UI: 6.72–12.04).

Compared to the status quo, the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of the RATIONS intervention was $289 per DALY averted (95% UI: 156–537) under the healthcare perspective and $229 (95% UI: 102–468) under the societal perspective. Both estimates are below the country-specific WTP threshold of $570 per DALY averted.

### Sensitivity analysis

One-way sensitivity analyses showed that the parameter with the greatest impact on the ICER was the six-month cost of nutritional support for HHCs, with ICERs ranging from $204 to $652 across the tested range ($20–$75). In threshold analysis, the RATIONS intervention remained cost-effective below the WTP when the monthly cost for HHCs was under $65. TB incidence also had a substantial effect, with ICERs ranging from $186 to $436 across the tested range. However, this was largely driven by the variation in the incidence rate in the first 5 years. When we held this period constant and only varied the incidence in the subsequent period between 65 and 390/100,000, the ICER range reduced to $248 to $302. The model was moderately sensitive to the age of the cohort and the protective effect of nutritional support on TB mortality. On threshold analysis, the WTP was met at the risk ratio for mortality of 0.98 (Supplementary figure 1). The effect of nutritional support on TB incidence had a smaller influence on the ICER, which ranged from $238 to $392 across the tested values. Other parameters—including the cost of nutritional support for PWTB, the probability of TB recurrence, the cost of TB treatment, the disability weight for post-TB lung disease, and the increased risk of post-TB mortality—had limited effects on the ICER (Table 4).

In two-way sensitivity analyses (Figure 2), the RATIONS intervention was cost-effective from the healthcare perspective, even at the lowest estimate of TB mortality reduction (RR: 0.85), as long as the six-month supplement cost per HHC did not exceed $44.2. Similarly, when assuming the lowest decrease in TB incidence (RR: 0.85), the RATIONS intervention remained below the WTP threshold at costs below $47. When considering the societal perspective, the corresponding values were $52 and $55. We conducted a two-way sensitivity analysis varying the risk ratios for TB mortality and TB incidence. The RATIONS intervention was the preferred strategy across nearly the entire parameter space, with usual care favored only when the RR of mortality exceeded 0.83 and the RR of incidence exceeded 0.78 (Figure 2b). When considering the societal perspective, the corresponding values were 0.82 and 0.81.

Lastly, in probabilistic sensitivity analysis, the RATIONS intervention was favored at a WTP of $570 in 98.5% and 99.5% of model simulations from the healthcare and societal perspectives, respectively (Figure 3). RATIONS was consistently preferable in >99% of iterations at a WTP of $598 and $530 from these perspectives, respectively.

## DISCUSSION

Nutritional interventions are often perceived to be cost-prohibitive. However, the RATIONS study has provided empirical evidence that low-cost nutritional support for HHCs of individuals diagnosed with TB could have a substantial impact on lowering the risk of incident TB in settings with high rates of multidimensional poverty and undernutrition. Our analysis suggests that an in-kind nutritional intervention modeled after the RATIONS study food basket could be cost-effective for reducing TB incidence and mortality in India, with a cost-effectiveness of $289 per DALY averted from a healthcare perspective and $229 per DALY averted from a societal perspective, when compared to no nutritional support. Our findings can help the NTEP consider the economics of implementing nutritional support to reduce the incidence of TB among HHCs.

In our analysis, the ICER was most sensitive to the cost of nutritional supplementation for HHCs. Even when we assumed the lowest possible effect of dietary interventions on incident TB disease, nutritional support would be cost-effective at $47 per recipient over six months, which is far higher than the reported cost of the intervention during the study. State and national governments are likely to enjoy economies of scale that could further lower the cost of the intervention.

While the RATIONS trial provided nutritional support to all PWTB in both arms, it was not designed to estimate the impact of nutrition on treatment outcomes among PWTB. To approximate this effect, we compared TB-related mortality in the RATIONS cohort to that observed in a cohort from the National TB Elimination Program in similar districts, yielding a risk ratio of 0.65 (95% CI: 0.49–0.85).(5) We acknowledge this is an indirect comparison that may be influenced by differences in implementation context and care quality and that causal inference is challenging. We therefore conducted sensitivity analyses varying this parameter across a wide range, including conservative estimates approaching no mortality benefit, to ensure our conclusions were robust. The ICER remained below the WTP threshold even when the relative reduction in mortality was assumed to be just 2%. Comparison to other evidence suggests the effect sizes we examined in these sensitivity analyses are credible. Indeed, despite being underpowered, a COCHRANE review of macronutrient supplementation estimated that macronutrient supplementation was associated with an RR of 0.34 (95% CI: 0.10–1.20) for TB mortality.(21) As nutritional interventions are scaled up programmatically, there may be opportunities to embed cluster-randomized studies that rigorously assess the impact of nutritional support on TB mortality.

Our analysis has several limitations. The effect parameters were drawn from a single study and may not be representative of India or even the entire state of Jharkhand, as noted above. We did not model the impact of nutritional interventions on treatment failure or loss to follow-up, even though these are plausible effects.(22) Additionally, our model does not explicitly capture potential benefits from intensified household visits under the nutritional support intervention, such as earlier TB detection and treatment initiation or improved adherence, which may further improve health outcomes. This Markov model focused on direct health benefits, but could not account for reductions in TB transmission and secondary TB episodes, but another model suggests that these would be reduced as well.(23) Further, we limited the reduction in TB incidence among HHCs to two years after exposure to match the duration of follow-up observed in the RATIONS study, making our estimates conservative. Our cost assumptions were limited to drug-susceptible TB, which is less costly to treat than drug-resistant TB.(15) Lastly, the model did not capture additional benefits of nutritional support on health and economic productivity.(24)

Public health investments to eliminate TB and undernutrition have historically provided some of the greatest returns on investment.(25, 26) Improvements in population-level nutrition and progress on social determinants of health likely contributed to the massive decline in TB incidence and mortality in the global North before the advent of antimicrobials.(27) India is well-positioned to institute a large-scale nutritional support program as it already has well-established infrastructure for delivering in-kind rations, mid-day meals, and nutritional counseling.(28–30) There are already plans to expand in-kind support through the Nikshay Mitra Program.(31)

In conclusion, our analysis projected that a RATIONS-style intervention would be cost-effective for populations with a high dual burden of TB and undernutrition in India and could drive large reductions in TB incidence and mortality among HHCs of PWTB.
